subject: Vocabulary
description: Common English idioms + their meanings; SSC + banking PYQ favorites

questions.stem: Meaning of idiom 'TO HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD':

options.option_text: To hurt someone physically with tools
To say or do exactly the right thing
To start a hammering project
To make a careless decision

questions.explanation: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD = to identify or describe something exactly correctly; pinpoint the truth. From carpentry — striking precisely on the nail. Common SSC PYQ idiom.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Meaning of idiom 'A BLESSING IN DISGUISE':

options.option_text: An obvious gift to be received
Something good that seemed bad first
A religious ceremony or ritual
A planned surprise for someone

questions.explanation: BLESSING IN DISGUISE = a misfortune that turns out to be beneficial later. 'Losing that job was a blessing in disguise — I got a better one.' Similar: 'silver lining' (good aspect of bad situation).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Meaning of idiom 'TO LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG':

options.option_text: To release a pet animal home
To accidentally reveal a secret
To change topic of discussion
To go on a hunting expedition

questions.explanation: LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG = reveal a secret (often by mistake). Origin: medieval traders allegedly substituted cats for piglets in bags at market — pulling the cat out exposed the fraud. PYQ-favourite idiom.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Meaning of idiom 'TO BURN THE MIDNIGHT OIL':

options.option_text: To work hard late into the night
To waste fuel resources at home
To celebrate a midnight party event
To be reckless with one's money

questions.explanation: BURN THE MIDNIGHT OIL = study or work late into the night. Origin: pre-electricity era, oil lamps used at night → burning the lamp's oil till midnight = working late. 'She burned the midnight oil to finish the report.'
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Meaning of idiom 'TO COST AN ARM AND A LEG':

options.option_text: To suffer a serious physical injury
To be very expensive (huge price)
To require great physical effort
To exhaust one's energy fully

questions.explanation: COST AN ARM AND A LEG = be very expensive. 'That car costs an arm and a leg.' Hyperbolic — implies you'd need to give up something as valuable as a body part. Synonym idioms: cost a fortune, cost a packet, pay through the nose.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Meaning of idiom 'TO BEAT AROUND THE BUSH':

options.option_text: To garden or trim hedges in yard
To avoid getting to the main point
To search for something with effort
To hunt small animals near house

questions.explanation: BEAT AROUND THE BUSH = to avoid coming to the point; to be evasive. Origin: medieval bird-hunting — beaters would strike bushes to flush birds out for hunters; the actual hunt came after, so 'beating around' was a precursor that delayed the main act. 'Stop beating around the bush + tell me directly.'

options.option_text: To accept something painful bravely
To shoot someone with a gun
To eat something extremely hot
To grit one's teeth from cold

questions.explanation: BITE THE BULLET = endure a painful or unpleasant situation that is unavoidable. Origin: pre-anaesthesia surgery — soldiers given a bullet (or leather strap) to bite during operation, to brace against pain. 'I had to bite the bullet + tell my boss the truth.'

questions.stem: Priya had promised to keep the engagement a secret, but she _____ when she told her cousin about the ceremony in excitement.

options.option_text: turned a blind eye to the whole situation
spilled the beans about the upcoming event
got cold feet at the very last moment
bit the dust just before the ceremony

questions.explanation: 'Spill the beans' means to accidentally or prematurely reveal a secret — exactly what Priya did by telling her cousin. Option C ('got cold feet') is tempting as it also involves a last-minute lapse, but it means becoming hesitant or nervous, not disclosing information.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the idiom 'TO GET COLD FEET'?

options.option_text: to develop a sudden physical ailment before an event
to become hesitant or anxious just before taking action
to feel uncomfortably cold during harsh winter weather
to run away from a physically exhausting task quickly

questions.explanation: 'Get cold feet' means to lose confidence or become nervous about a commitment, especially right before carrying it out. Option A exploits the literal image of falling ill (physical cold), while Option D confuses emotional avoidance with fleeing a physical challenge — both incorrect.

questions.stem: In which of the following sentences is the idiom 'TURN A BLIND EYE' used correctly?

options.option_text: The supervisor turned a blind eye and promoted him swiftly
The inspector turned a blind eye to the safety violations
She turned a blind eye to study harder for the upcoming exam
He turned a blind eye at the vivid paintings in the gallery

questions.explanation: 'Turn a blind eye' means to deliberately ignore something improper or wrong. In option B, the inspector knowingly overlooks safety violations — the correct usage. Option D is tempting because 'eyes' and 'gallery' collocate naturally, but the idiom specifically implies wilful disregard of wrongdoing, not literal vision.

questions.stem: The idiom 'TO BITE THE DUST' most aptly describes which of the following scenarios?

options.option_text: a miner who carefully excavates dry, dusty terrain daily
a once-popular brand that lost all its market share
a farmer who prepares parched land ahead of monsoon rains
a soldier who cleans his rifle while lying on the ground

questions.explanation: 'Bite the dust' means to fail completely, be defeated, or cease to exist. A brand losing all market share is a classic example of total defeat. Options A, C, and D are deliberately designed to exploit the literal imagery of dust and ground — none involve failure or defeat.

questions.stem: In which of the following sentences is the idiom 'TO CUT CORNERS' used correctly?

options.option_text: The stylist cut corners of the hair evenly for a neat look
The contractor cut corners to meet deadlines, ignoring safety
She cut corners of the fabric while stitching the costume
The athlete cut corners on the track to complete the lap

questions.explanation: 'Cut corners' means to reduce effort, quality, or cost by taking shortcuts, often at the expense of proper standards. The contractor skipping safety checks is a textbook usage. Options A and C involve literal cutting of physical corners, and option D describes an actual spatial shortcut in running — all incorrect idiomatic usage.

questions.stem: The idiom 'TO HAVE A CHIP ON ONE'S SHOULDER' best describes a person who ___.

options.option_text: openly brags about achievements to impress colleagues around
harbours deep resentment and is easily drawn into conflicts
remains calm and composed under intense workplace pressure
takes on extra responsibilities without seeking any credit

questions.explanation: 'A chip on one's shoulder' refers to a persistent sense of grievance or inferiority that makes a person resentful and combative. Option A (bragging) is the most common confusion — that describes 'blowing one's own trumpet'. Option D, selflessly taking on burdens, is the near opposite of the chip-bearer's resentful posture.

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the meaning of the idiom 'TO BURN ONE'S BOATS'?

options.option_text: to damage another person's property in a fit of rage
to take a drastic, irreversible decision eliminating any retreat
to endure severe hardship while single-mindedly pursuing a goal
to abandon a profitable venture under mounting social pressure

questions.explanation: 'Burn one's boats' (also 'burn one's bridges') means to take an action that makes it impossible to reverse course. The phrase originates from military tactics where commanders burned their fleet so troops had no option but to fight forward. Option C (enduring hardship) is the most seductive distractor because it implies commitment, but critically lacks the element of irreversibility that defines this idiom.
